name: The Yellow Christmas Tree of Stanyan Street

location.address: 1221 Stanyan Street, in front of the house

verified_sources: https://sfpublicworks.org/services/significant-and-landmark-trees (SF Public Works official list of designated Landmark Trees: '1221 Stanyan Street: New Zealand Christmas Tree')

http://www.sftrees.com/blog/2016/5/30/my-favorite-tree (Mike Sullivan, 2016: yellow mutation from Motiti Island 1940, cutting planted in front of 1221 Stanyan by Victor Reiter's family, 'more than 70 years later thriving', blooms yellow around Memorial Day, seen from the street)
https://www.sfenvironment.org/landmark-tree-program (seen only via search result; page 403s to fetchers; designation by Urban Forestry Council 2019, unanimous vote)
access: Visible from the public sidewalk on Stanyan Street; it stands in front of a private home, so look from the pavement only.
transport: Muni N Judah or 6/7 to Haight St and Stanyan, short walk (stop not verified)
verify_notes: Official Landmark Tree (2019). Rare YELLOW-flowering cultivar of the common red NZ Christmas tree: natural mutation found 1940 on Motiti Island NZ; Victor Reiter obtained a cutting in the late 1950s and planted it in front of the family home. Blooms around Memorial Day. Pin is the geocoded building at 1221 Stanyan (Nominatim), not the trunk; aerial not checked, so approximate. Alive: lifecheck RECENT, iNaturalist observation 2026-04-19 within radius (not proven same trunk): https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/351189918. Age: no source dates the tree itself beyond the late-1950s planting per Sullivan. Different from the CA Big Trees NZ Christmas tree champion lead. Front of a dwelling: viewing place is the pavement; do not imply entry. Girth unknown.
story:
New Zealand Christmas trees flower red. This one flowers yellow. The yellow form began as a natural mutation, found on Motiti Island in New Zealand's Bay of Plenty in 1940, in a species that otherwise blooms crimson.

Victor Reiter got hold of a cutting in the late 1950s and his family planted it in front of their home at 1221 Stanyan Street, on the edge of Cole Valley. The local tree writer Mike Sullivan, writing in 2016, called it his favourite tree in the city and found it thriving more than seventy years after that first yellow plant turned up. In 2019 the Urban Forestry Council voted unanimously to make it an official Landmark Tree.

Its moment comes around Memorial Day, at the end of May, when it blooms, and the flowers can still cover it in late June. Every other New Zealand Christmas tree you pass in the city flowers red.

This is a front garden, not a park, and the right way to see it is from the public pavement on Stanyan Street, without stepping off it. Our pin marks the address rather than the trunk.

The city still lists it among its landmark trees, but the newest dated photograph we have found is from June 2012, when it was in full yellow flower. Nobody has published its girth. If you photograph it from the pavement in flower, send it to us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it in early summer by its yellow flowers, where the city's other New Zealand Christmas trees bloom red. It stands in front of the house at 1221 Stanyan Street; look from the pavement.

best_time.label: late May into June, when it blooms yellow instead of red

name: The Canary Palms of Quesada Avenue

location.address: Quesada Avenue median, just west of 3rd Street

https://www.sanfranciscostory.com/quesada-gardens/ (fetched directly: median planted around 1920 with Canary Island Date Palms, same as Dolores Street; palms survived the twentieth century)

Planting date conflict: sanfranciscostory.com says about 1920; a search summary (lead only) says about 1932. Do not narrow. Pin: Nominatim places Quesada Avenue between roughly 37.7299,-122.3854 and 37.7331,-122.3911; I set an approximate mid-block point, NOT checked on aerial imagery. lifecheck NONE at pin: alive evidence is only the official list and undated-recent articles; flag. Girth and height unknown.
story:
Thirteen Canary Island date palms line the median of Quesada Avenue in the Bayview, and San Francisco counts all thirteen as one Landmark Tree. Public Works lists them that way: the Quesada Street median, from just west of 3rd Street to the dead end, 13 palms.

They are the same species as the far better known palms down the middle of Dolores Street. Local history has the Quesada median planted with them around 1920. One account puts it closer to 1932, and we have not been able to settle which, so call them roughly a century old, give or take a decade.

What they have seen since is most of the Bayview's twentieth century, and they outlasted all of it; the city's current landmark list still carries all thirteen. A palm of this kind holds no rings to count, and nobody has published the height or the girth of any of the thirteen, so the age rests on the planting date alone.

This is a street, not a park, and that is the appeal: the whole landmark stands on one compact block, so there is one place to go and thirteen trees to count. Walk the sidewalk rather than the median itself.

Our pin is a mid-block point that has not been checked against aerial imagery, so treat it as the street rather than a spot. The 3rd Street end is the easy one to find. If you know when these palms were really planted, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the row of thirteen Canary Island date palms down the median of Quesada Avenue, running west from 3rd Street to the dead end.

name: The Centennial Tree of the Presidio

location.address: Main Parade Ground, Main Post, Presidio of San Francisco

verified_sources: https://presidio.gov/explore/blog/discover-eight-presidio-memorials-and-monuments (Presidio Trust, the ground's manager: Angelo Beretta, post trader, planted three eucalyptus in front of his store at the Main Post in 1876; Army removed two when it enlarged the parade ground; the third was preserved by a special act of Congress and became the Centennial Tree)

https://www.nps.gov/goga/learn/photosmultimedia/now-and-then-presidio.htm (NPS Golden Gate NRA, page last updated 2025-03-26: planted 1876 in honour of his three daughters; the Centennial Tree 'still stands near the center of the parade ground')
http://www.sftrees.com/new-page-1 (Mike Sullivan, San Francisco Trees: blue gum, planted 4 July 1876, plaque at the base, gift of Beretta's descendants in 1976)
access: Free; open lawn on the Main Parade Ground of the Presidio, a public national park site. Presidio Trust publishes no hours for the tree.
transport: Presidio Go shuttle or Muni 43 to the Main Post, short walk across the parade ground (stop not verified)
verify_notes: Dated, documented planting: 4 July 1876 by Angelo Beretta, the Presidio's post trader, to mark the centennial of the Declaration of Independence. Sources disagree on the three trees (one for each of his children per Presidio Trust; three daughters per NPS and sftrees); do not state which. Two of three removed when the Army enlarged the parade ground; the survivor kept 'by a special act of Congress' (Presidio Trust wording, no second source for the Act). Plaque at the base: 'planted July 4, 1876 by Angelo Beretta Post Trader, gift from his family July 4, 1976' (Commons file Presidio_of_SF_Centennial_Tree_plaque.JPG; HMDB 284771 reads the same but 403s to fetchers). Presidio Trust planning (Main Post Update, 2010) says to maintain it as a symbolic object (seen only via search summary). Presidio forest context: the Army plantation of 1886 onward is younger than this tree, so this predates the forest. Alive: NPS 2025 'still stands'; lifecheck RECENT 2026-08-29 near the pin (iNaturalist, not confirmed as this trunk). Pin: NO coordinate found (Nominatim empty, Commons plaque photo not geotagged); the point is my estimate for the centre of the Main Parade Ground, so approximate. Size: no girth or height in any source. sftrees calls it more historically significant than visually spectacular. Photo hunt, not done by me: Commons has Presidio_of_SF_Centennial_Tree_1.JPG and _2.JPG (BrokenSphere, CC BY-SA 3.0, 2009-02-08), unchecked for which trunk. A younger 'Bicentennial Tree' (HMDB 284786) stands nearby, not this tree.
story:
This eucalyptus is older than the forest around it. Angelo Beretta, the Presidio's post trader, planted it on 4 July 1876 to mark the hundredth birthday of the Declaration of Independence, a decade before the Army began the plantation that grew into the Presidio's woods.

He planted three, in front of his store at the Main Post. When the Army enlarged the parade ground, two of them came out. The third stayed. The Presidio Trust, which manages the ground, says it was spared by a special act of Congress; no second source names the act, so that detail rests on the Trust's word.

A century later, on 4 July 1976, Beretta's family gave the plaque at its base, which records the planting date and his name. That plaque matters more than usual, because a younger Bicentennial Tree stands nearby and is easy to take for this one.

The National Park Service said in 2025 that the Centennial Tree still stands near the centre of the parade ground that cost it its two companions.

Nobody has published a girth or a height, and one San Francisco tree writer rates it more for its history than its size. The pin is our estimate for the middle of the Main Parade Ground rather than a surveyed point, so walk to the centre of the lawn and look for the plaque. If you have measured the trunk, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the plaque at its base, with Angelo Beretta's name and the date July 4, 1876. It stands near the centre of the Main Parade Ground; the younger Bicentennial Tree nearby is a different tree.

Search summary (pointer only, not a page I read): scheduled for removal in 1999 for new construction, owner built around it and signed a tree easement with Friends of the Urban Forest. Age: only 'over 100 years' from the blog; age_max left null. Girth: DataSF mapdbh 72 in = 183 cm diameter times pi = 574 cm; diameter at breast height of a buttressed fig, register estimate, never confirmed by a second source; sanity plausible for a big fig. Alive: lifecheck RECENT, iNaturalist observation 2025-02-23; but branch failures reported 2009 to 2010, so condition may have changed. Pin: DataSF coordinate on the side yard; address mismatch (Public Works lists 3555 Cesar Chavez, DataSF 1580 Valencia; both describe the same corner per sftrees). Private ground; that it is seen from the sidewalk is inferred from the blog's marker 'below the tree' and sftrees' street-side location, no source states it outright. View-only: pin on the viewing place (Valencia St frontage). Worth the visit: the largest fig of its kind in the city. One credible US source (government list) plus independent blog corroboration.
